title: Group Photo Poses That Are Actually Fun and Awesome
summary: Group photo poses for every headcount: triangles for small groups, staggered rows for big ones, candid setups, team photos and blink-free math.
body_markdown:
## Great group photos are a matter of preparation


Someone says "squeeze in," the phone comes out, and you get a flat line with two faces half-hidden and one person mid-blink. Group photos are an arrangement problem first. Get the shape right for the headcount and the rest gets easier.


## Small groups (3 to 5): build a triangle


With three to five people, use a triangle: the tallest person in the middle, the others angled in so heads sit at different heights. It's the go-to shape for[family photography services](https://www.snappr.com/blog/family-photography-services) sessions too.


• The lean-in: everyone turns their shoulders toward the center and closes the gaps.


• Seated and standing: one or two people sit on a bench or low wall, the rest stand behind.


• The walk: the group strolls toward the camera, chatting. Canon Europe's group portrait guide quotes family photographer Helen Bartlett recommending movement like this to add energy.


## Medium groups (6 to 15): rows that don't look like a lineup


Past six people, you need rows, and two is usually enough. Put taller people at the back, shorter or seated ones in front, then shift the back row half a step sideways so each face sits in a gap.


A V-formation beats a straight line: one or two people at the point, everyone else fanning out behind. Or bookend the back row with the tallest people at each end.


For team-style shots, Canon Europe cites The Times chief sports photographer Marc Aspland, who has the back row stand, the front row kneel, the captain in the middle of the back row, and the camera low, almost level with the front row's heads.


Kids in front, a toddler on a hip, taller adults behind. Ten faces, no one hidden.


## Large groups (15 and up): go up, not wide


Build height, not width: stairs, bleachers, a hillside, or chairs in front of a bench, with three or more tiers. Then shoot from a stepladder or balcony so you see every face over the row in front. Canon Europe quotes Aspland recommending f/5.6 or f/8 so front and back rows both stay sharp.


Big groups also need more frames. CSIRO researchers Nic Svenson and Piers Barnes worked out the math, and ABC Science reported it won them a 2006 Ig Nobel Prize: for groups under 20, divide the headcount by three to get the number of shots you need, or by two in bad light. By around 50 people, Svenson told ABC, a single unspoiled frame is a lost cause.


## Stagger heights so no face gets hidden


Each face should sit in the gap between two heads in the row in front, never directly behind one. Check from the camera, not from inside the group.


• Seat the front row on chairs, a bench or the edge of a stage.


• Have tall people widen their stance instead of slouching.


• Lift small kids onto hips.


• Ask everyone to push their chin slightly forward and down for a cleaner jawline.


The same stagger logic runs through our[prom photo poses](https://www.snappr.com/blog/prom-photo-poses) for friend groups and our[graduation photo poses](https://www.snappr.com/blog/graduation-photo-poses) for cap-and-gown lineups.


Shot from above, with a kneeling front row, 35 faces all find a gap. That's the whole trick.


## Candid group shots that still look planned


Canon Europe quotes Bartlett saying the frame after the formal portrait usually wins, as people turn to each other and laugh. So keep shooting. Prompts help: hug the person on your left, walk ten steps and turn around.


Squeeze in after the formal shot. The huddle frame is usually the keeper.


For blinks, wedding photographer Sanjay Jogia's fix in the same Canon guide is to have everyone close their eyes, count down to one, then take three shots about half a second apart.


Good news for the camera-shy: in experiments published in Psychological Science, UC San Diego researchers Drew Walker and Edward Vul found people were rated more attractive in a group than alone.


## Team and office group photos


Team photos follow the same rules with a tighter brief: agree on a color palette and pick a background that says something about the business.


These photos work hard on About pages. In a Nielsen Norman Group eyetracking study, one user spent 10% more time looking at a company's team portraits than reading the biographies, even though the text took up 316% more space. Pair a strong team shot with consistent[corporate headshots](https://www.snappr.com/blog/corporate-headshots) and the page does its job at a glance.


Real coworkers in their own office. On an About page, this is the photo people look at.


## Let someone else hold the camera


Whoever knows how to arrange everyone usually ends up behind the phone and out of the shot. A professional handles the rows, the extra frames and the editing, so everyone makes the picture.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What are the best group photo poses for small groups?


For three to five people, a triangle works best, with the tallest person in the middle and the others angled in at different heights. Mix seated and standing, or have the group walk toward the camera.


### How do you pose a large group photo?


Build height with stairs, bleachers or chairs and a bench, arrange three or more staggered rows, and shoot from slightly above. Put each face in a gap between two heads in front.


### How many pictures should you take of a group?


CSIRO researchers found that for groups under 20, you should divide the number of people by three to get the shots needed for one blink-free frame, or by two in poor light.


### How do you stop faces being hidden in group photo poses?


Stagger the rows so every face sits between two heads in front of it. Seat the first row, check from the camera position, and shift people half a step until every face is clear.


## Sources


1.[Canon Europe, How to shoot standout group portraits](https://www.canon-europe.com/get-inspired/tips-and-techniques/group-portraits/) : Helen Bartlett on movement and the shot after the formal portrait; Marc Aspland on two-row team layouts, low camera angle and f/5.6 to f/8; Sanjay Jogia's eyes-closed countdown and three shots half a second apart


2.[ABC Science, Blink-free photos win Ig Nobel (2006)](https://www.abc.net.au/science/articles/2006/10/06/1752039.htm) : CSIRO's Nic Svenson and Piers Barnes on dividing headcount by three (or two in bad light) for groups under 20, and the 50-person limit


3.[Association for Psychological Science, Cheerleader Effect: Why People Are More Beautiful in Groups](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/cheerleader-effect-why-people-are-more-beautiful-in-groups.html) : Walker and Vul (UC San Diego) findings published in Psychological Science


4.[Nielsen Norman Group, Photos as Web Content](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/photos-as-web-content/) : eyetracking finding that a user spent 10% more time on team portraits than bios that took 316% more space
